memory_update.text: For the Technology theme, the most researchable near-term chain is AI infrastructure rather than generic technology: AI workloads -> hyperscaler capex -> accelerators/HBM -> advanced package substrates/ABF -> passives/MLCCs -> networking/optics -> rack-scale integration -> power/cooling -> downstream AI adopters.

Advanced package substrates and ABF build-up film are priority chokepoint nodes because AI package complexity, supplier concentration, long qualification, yield learning, and material allocation may constrain effective capacity.

High-end AI-server MLCCs and upstream dielectric powders are low-attention bottleneck candidates; the chain may hide value in passive components and specialty materials rather than visible AI semiconductor names.
Networking and rack-scale integration are emerging AI infrastructure bottleneck nodes, especially around 800G/1.6T switching, optical connectivity, and EMS/ODM integration.
Track customer prepayments, co-funded capacity, substrate/ABF allocation, MLCC lead times, and explicit AI/HPC commentary in earnings as catalysts that can validate or falsify bottleneck status.
Track downstream AI productivity evidence because second-order AI adopters may become a separate Technology sub-theme if efficiency gains and margin expansion become visible in reported financials.

Need primary-source verification from annual reports, earnings calls, investor decks, customer announcements, and capacity disclosures for each low-attention supplier before moving from Layer 2A map to company ranking.
Need a dedicated power/cooling/grid follow-up; this run includes those nodes as plausible AI infrastructure constraints but lacks direct source evidence in the supplied external context.
Need distributor/channel research to test whether allocation relationships in passives, optics, substrates, and power components create hidden bottleneck value.

The candidate chunk forms a coherent physical AI infrastructure subtheme: ABF materials, high-end substrates, high-end MLCCs, MLCC dielectric powders, and process-control tools all connect to rising package complexity, power density, and yield constraints.

4078.JP Sakai Chemical should remain in the underfollowed lane, but its relationship is still a hypothesis until filings confirm electronic-materials revenue mix, BaTiO3 capability, and MLCC customer exposure.

AJINY Ajinomoto is a reference ABF material node rather than a pure-play AI name; the key research issue is whether ABF economics are large enough and durable enough to matter inside a diversified food and specialty-materials company.

MRAAY Murata, TTDKY TDK, and TYOYY Taiyo Yuden should be tracked as MLCC/passive-component candidates, but Layer 3 needs application-level evidence separating AI-server demand from broader electronics recovery.

4062.JP Ibiden has the strongest external substrate-bottleneck narrative in this chunk, but the current evidence includes a specialist external source and should be upgraded with company filings on customer advances, capex, and substrate-segment growth.

3037.TW Unimicron and 8046.TW Nan Ya PCB are underfollowed substrate candidates because Taiwan PCB/substrate exposure may be misclassified as cyclical hardware rather than AI package substrate capacity.

KLAC is a reference leader for complexity and yield-control monetization; it helps validate the process-control node but is less aligned with the underfollowed small/mid-cap discovery lens due to high attention and mega-cap status.

Current market caps, liquidity, listing accessibility, ADR conventions, and US investability for Japanese and Taiwanese candidates remain unverified and should be checked before Layer 3 prioritization.
Customer-supplier links among Ajinomoto, Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, Murata, TDK, Taiyo Yuden, and Sakai Chemical are not yet sufficiently proven by primary sources in this run.

Need primary-source validation for AI/HPC revenue mix, segment margin expansion, backlog, utilization, lead-time extension, allocation, pricing, customer prepayments, and qualification cycles across all material, substrate, and MLCC candidates.

VSH should remain in the AI-server passive-components funnel only as a speculative-shadow candidate until filings, product specs, or customer evidence confirm AI-server-grade MLCC or adjacent high-reliability passive exposure.

ARW maps best as a second-order distribution and shortage-signal node, not as a direct AI hardware bottleneck; prioritize lead-time, allocation, book-to-bill, inventory, and supplier line-card evidence.
AVT maps best as a second-order distribution and supply-chain visibility node; it requires transcript and line-card validation before being upgraded from underfollowed inference.

4092.JP is a potential MLCC dielectric-powder upstream node, but the key survival test is whether its BESPA or related products are qualified into high-end thin-layer MLCCs used by AI-server component suppliers.
300285.SZ is a possible China-localization MLCC materials node; evidence must separate commodity ceramic-material exposure from high-end hydrothermal BaTiO3 powder suitable for thin-layer MLCCs.

009150.KS should serve as the reference MLCC benchmark in this chunk; its evidence package should be used to define what credible AI-server-grade MLCC exposure looks like for smaller or less-followed peers.
No provided primary-source evidence yet validates direct AI-server customer wins, AI-server MLCC shipment mix, or data-center revenue contribution for VSH, 4092.JP, 300285.SZ, ARW, AVT, or 009150.KS.
Market-cap buckets, liquidity, current valuation, analyst coverage, and US investability for non-US tickers in this chunk still require verification before later Serenity layers.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Initial Layer 2A industry-chain map for the broad Technology theme, narrowed to AI infrastructure and second-order AI adoption because the cached Layer 1 universe and external evidence cluster around AI compute, advanced packaging, MLCC/passives, networking, data-center integration, and downstream AI productivity adopters. The highest-bottleneck nodes appear to be advanced package substrates, ABF build-up film, high-end AI-server MLCC/passive components, process-control/inspection, and rack-scale networking/optical integration. This map deliberately avoids letting obvious mega-cap AI chip and cloud leaders dominate; it highlights low-attention suppliers, substrate makers, specialty materials, passive components, EMS/ODM integration, qualification gates, and downstream adopters as possible hidden value nodes.

supply_chain_map.node: AI workload demand and downstream enterprise AI adoption
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Enterprise adoption and agentic/automation workloads drive the need for more compute, networking, storage, power density, and software integration. External evidence also suggests that some lasting value may accrue to companies deploying AI effectively, not only infrastructure suppliers.

Large cloud and hyperscale buyers determine accelerator volumes, rack-scale architecture, networking standards, supplier qualification, and advance payments to constrained upstream suppliers. Customer co-funding or advance payments can signal true supply scarcity.

Accelerators remain the visible demand driver, but the Serenity lens treats them more as the pull-through source for upstream constraints in packaging, substrates, memory, passives, power, and networking rather than the only investable node.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM and advanced memory stack supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-bandwidth memory is required for large AI training and inference systems. It interacts with advanced packaging capacity and substrate complexity, but the provided evidence set does not include enough current HBM-specific source support to rank it above substrate/passive bottlenecks in this run.

Advanced substrates connect large AI accelerators, HBM, and package-level power/signal routing. External evidence claims each AI chip generation requires more substrate layers, larger body sizes, finer features, and embedded power components, shrinking the supplier set at viable yields.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF build-up film and substrate dielectric materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: ABF film is a critical material for high-end package substrates. The cached universe identifies Ajinomoto as a reference leader, while external evidence frames ABF allocation as a gate for new substrate entrants and a source of incumbent advantage for existing high-volume customers.

supply_chain_map.node: Substrate customer qualification and yield-learning loop
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: This is not regulation in the legal sense, but a certification/qualification gate. Long customer qualification cycles, commercial-yield hurdles, and accumulated yield-learning data can protect incumbents and slow new capacity from becoming effective capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: High-end AI-server MLCCs and passive components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerator boards and dense server power-delivery networks require high-capacitance, low-ESR/ESL, small-form-factor passive components. Cached Layer 1 highlights Murata, Taiyo Yuden, TDK, Yageo, Vishay, and upstream dielectric-powder suppliers as nodes where low-attention bottlenecks may hide.

supply_chain_map.node: MLCC dielectric powders and specialty ceramic materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Upstream barium titanate and related dielectric powders can be hidden chokepoints for high-end MLCCs. Cached Layer 1 identifies Sakai Chemical as a low-attention candidate whose AI relevance is hidden inside MLCC dielectric powder supply.

supply_chain_map.node: Semiconductor process control, inspection, and metrology
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Rising chip, memory, substrate, and packaging complexity increases the need for inspection and yield-control tools. Cached Layer 1 uses KLA as a reference leader for monetizing complexity rather than end demand directly.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging equipment and test infrastructure
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As packaging complexity rises, bottlenecks can emerge in inspection, bonding, lithography-adjacent packaging steps, substrate test, burn-in, and reliability qualification. The provided evidence is more general than company-specific for this node, so it remains an inference node for follow-up.

AI clusters increasingly shift constraints from only GPUs/memory toward networking throughput, high-bandwidth switching, and rack-scale integration. External evidence specifically mentions 800G and upcoming 1.6T switch deployments as a catalyst area.

Higher cluster scale and faster interconnect requirements increase demand for optical modules, optical engines, connectors, substrates, and testing. This node may hide low-attention suppliers one or two steps away from visible networking vendors.

supply_chain_map.node: Rack-scale systems integration, EMS, and ODM manufacturing
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI infrastructure is increasingly bought as rack-scale systems rather than isolated boards. External evidence identifies Celestica as exposed to high-speed switches, optical connectivity, and customized rack-scale infrastructure, indicating that EMS/ODM integration can become a bottleneck node.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center power delivery and board-level power density
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Accelerator density raises requirements for VRMs, power modules, capacitors, inductors, connectors, PSUs, and thermal-power architecture. Cached Layer 1 repeatedly ties MLCCs and passive components to AI-server board power delivery.

Higher rack densities create cooling constraints. The provided evidence set does not contain direct sourced claims on liquid cooling, so this node is included as a technology-chain inference requiring follow-up source verification.

supply_chain_map.node: Power grid interconnection and data-center energy availability
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI data-center growth can be limited by utility interconnection queues, generation capacity, transformers, substations, and local permitting. This is a plausible technology bottleneck but not directly evidenced in the supplied search context, so it is marked for verification.

supply_chain_map.node: Distributor and allocation channels for constrained electronics components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: When passives, substrates, optical components, or power components tighten, authorized distributors and allocation relationships can determine who gets supply. This is a low-attention Serenity node, but current evidence in this run is insufficient for company mapping.

supply_chain_map.node: AI software workflow integration and productivity capture
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: External Morgan Stanley/Eaton Vance evidence argues that second-order beneficiaries may be companies that deploy AI to improve workflows, margins, and labor productivity. This node matters because the technology theme may broaden beyond infrastructure bottlenecks into adopters.
